question: A press release about a blood-thinning pill, written the way many are. Which number makes it sound better than it is?
answer: The 33%. If 3 in 100 untreated patients would have a stroke and the pill brings it to 2, that is a third fewer strokes, but one person in 100 helped against two harmed by bleeding. A review of leading medical journals found about one article in three mixed formats like this.
move: Put the good news and the bad news in the same units before comparing.
ask: When someone shows me pros and cons, are both in the same kind of number?

scene.head: Press release
scene.title: New pill cuts stroke risk
scene.body: In the trial, the new pill cut the risk of stroke by 33%. Major bleeding was uncommon, occurring in 2 extra patients per 100.

phrases.text: cut the risk of stroke by 33%
phrases.plain: prevented 1 stroke in 100 patients, 3 down to 2
phrases.why: A relative cut. A third of a small risk is a small number of people.

phrases.plain: Bleeding serious enough to need care
phrases.why: In trials, major is a defined grade of harm, not a nosebleed.

phrases.plain: twice as common as the strokes prevented
phrases.why: The harm is given as a count, so it sounds small. Put in the same units, it is bigger.

scene.ask: Benefit and harm are in different units. Which one flatters?
scene.watch: Ask for every result as people per 100. A percentage cut needs its starting point.

reference: Sedrakyan & Shih, Improving depiction of benefits and harms: analyses of studies of well-known therapeutics and review of high-impact medical journals, Medical Care, 2007
